chapters.weekHtml:
Week Read Build
1 Smith chapters 1 to 7, through HelloSilicon Assembly 101 on ARM64, natively on the Mac. By hand: a hello world that uses only the write and exit syscalls, strlen, memcpy, a loop that sums an array, and a recursive fib. Call each one from a C main and step through it in lldb.
2 Jorgensen, the chapters on instructions, control flow, functions and system services The same five programs in x86-64, in the Linux VM, with nasm and gdb. Put both versions side by side and write down where the arguments live, how the return address is saved and how the stack is aligned.
3 to 4 Computer Enhance 8086 interlude, first half 8086 decoder in C. Feed it the course's listings, produce byte-identical reassembly via nasm.
5 Computer Enhance second half 8086 simulator: registers, flags, memory, jumps. Run the course's programs. Print estimated cycles.
6 CS:APP chapter 3, sections 3.1 to 3.8 Bomb Lab in the Linux VM. Pure disassembly reading, no source.
7 CS:APP 3.10 (buffer overflow), chapter 7 Attack Lab. Then build your phase 2 JSON parser as three .o files linked through clang. Inspect the driver's ld invocation and identify its runtime inputs. Read the ELF with readelf -a.
8 ARM A64 guide chapters on registers, load/store and branches, Apple's ARM64 ABI page Read clang's ARM64 output at -O0 and -O2 for your phase 2 arena and JSON parser. Pick one hot function, rewrite it by hand in ARM64, and benchmark it against clang's version.
chapters.sourceText:
Goal: write small programs in ARM64 and x86-64 assembly by hand, then read both fluently enough to look at any C function in Compiler Explorer and say what it does. Know what a stack frame, a calling convention, a relocation and a dynamic symbol are because you have stepped through them. Ship hand-written assembly on both ISAs and an 8086 decoder and simulator. **Builds on:** phase 1 (what an instruction is) and phase 2 (pointers, stack and heap). **Adds:** writing and reading ARM64 and x86-64 assembly, calling conventions, linking. ### Primary resources - **Assembly 101 on ARM64, natively on your Mac:** Stephen Smith, *Programming with 64-Bit ARM Assembly Language* (Apress, 2020), together with the HelloSilicon repo, https://github.com/below/HelloSilicon. The repo ports every example in the book to Apple Silicon and notes each place where macOS differs from Linux. Chapters 1 to 7 in week 1: registers, loading and adding, the tools, branches and loops, memory, functions and the stack, OS calls. Type every program, build it with `as` and `ld` or through `clang`, and step through it in `lldb`. - **Assembly 101 on x86-64:** Ed Jorgensen, *x86-64 Assembly Language Programming with Ubuntu*, free PDF at http://www.egr.unlv.edu/\~ed/assembly64.pdf. In week 2 you redo the week 1 programs in x86-64 in the Linux VM. The book uses yasm. nasm accepts the same syntax for everything you write here. - **Casey Muratori, Computer Enhance, "Interlude: 8086 decoding and simulation"** (part 1 of the Performance-Aware Programming course, https://www.computerenhance.com, paid subscription, 15 USD per month). This is the best on-ramp to instruction encoding that exists. You write a decoder for real 8086 machine code, then a simulator, then estimate cycle counts. Casey's reasoning about why the ISA looks the way it does is the actual lesson. - **CS:APP chapter 3** (machine-level representation of programs) for x86-64. Do the Bomb Lab and the Attack Lab from https://csapp.cs.cmu.edu/3e/labs.html. They are the two best assembly exercises ever designed and they are free. - **CS:APP chapter 7** (linking). Read it in week 7 while building a multi-file program by hand with `clang -c` and `ld`. - **Compiler Explorer**, https://godbolt.org, open all day every day. Compile with `-O0`, then `-O2`, then an explicit CPU target, and compare. On Compiler Explorer, `-march=native` refers to its compilation host, not your laptop. - **ARM64 reference:** the Apple Silicon documentation is thin, so use the ARM "Learn the architecture: A64 Instruction Set" guide on developer.arm.com, Apple's "Writing ARM64 code for Apple platforms" page on developer.apple.com for the ABI differences, and Compiler Explorer with `armv8-a clang`. Keep all three open whenever you read ARM64 output. ### Beginner bridge: instruction set, ABI, file format - **ISA:** which instructions the CPU executes. ARM64 and x86-64 are different ISAs. - **ABI:** how separately compiled code agrees on arguments, return values, saved registers and stack alignment. Two OSes on the same ISA can use different ABIs. - **Object format:** how code, symbols and relocations are stored in a file. Linux uses ELF; macOS uses Mach-O. Start with one assembly `add` called from C. Use `clang` to assemble and link so its driver supplies runtime startup files and libraries. Once that works, inspect the commands with `clang -###`; direct `ld` is a later linking exercise, not the default way to link a libc program. Apple raw syscalls are an educational experiment, not a stable application interface. Prefer libc calls for normal macOS assembly. Install `nasm` in your chosen Ubuntu x86 environment with `sudo apt install nasm` before the x86 exercises. A normal ARM64 Linux guest does not automatically execute x86 binaries; use the explicitly configured emulation environment or native laptop. Use the [official LLDB/GDB command map](https://lldb.llvm.org/use/map.html) when a debugger command differs. **Checkpoint:** explain why valid ARM64 instructions can still crash when called with the wrong ABI. Preserve callee-saved registers and demonstrate a nested call before attempting recursion. ### What you are actually learning **A function call is a protocol, not magic.** The System V ABI on x86-64 Linux and macOS says: first six integer arguments go in `rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9`, return value in `rax`, `rsp` points to the stack top, `rbp` is an optional frame pointer, callee must preserve `rbx, rbp, r12 to r15`. Everything about "the stack" follows from that: ``` caller: higher addresses push args 7+ (if any) ┌─────────────────┐ call f ; pushes return addr │ caller's frame │ ├─────────────────┤ f: │ return address │ ◄─ pushed by `call` push rbp ; save old frame ├─────────────────┤ mov rbp, rsp ; new frame base │ saved rbp │ ◄─ rbp points here sub rsp, 32 ; room for locals ├─────────────────┤ ... ; locals at [rbp-8], │ local a │ ; [rbp-16], ... │ local b │ mov rsp, rbp ; drop locals │ (padding) │ ◄─ rsp points here pop rbp ; restore caller └─────────────────┘ ret ; pops return addr lower addresses ``` A stack-buffer overflow can overwrite neighboring locals or saved control data, including a return address in the lab's layout. Not every overflow reaches that address. The Attack Lab supplies deliberately vulnerable programs to study the mechanism. Recursion is just this frame stacked N times. A stack overflow is running out of the region. **The compiler is a rewriting machine and `-O2` is aggressive.** Things you will see in Compiler Explorer and should be able to name: inlining, loop unrolling, strength reduction (`x * 8` becomes `x << 3`), dead store elimination, tail calls, vectorization (phase 4), and the compiler deleting your whole benchmark because the result was unused. This last one is why every benchmark needs a sink. **Linking turns object files into a program by resolving names to addresses.** ```mermaid flowchart LR A[main.c] -->|clang -c| B[main.o
has main, needs parse] C[json.c] -->|clang -c| D[json.o
has parse, needs memcpy] B --> L[ld] D --> L E[libc.so
has memcpy] -.->|dynamic| L L --> F[app] F -.->|at run time| G[loader maps libc.so
patches GOT/PLT] ``` Each `.o` has sections (`.text`, `.data`, `.rodata`, `.bss`), a symbol table, and relocations: "at offset 0x2f in .text, write the address of `parse`." Static linking resolves all of them at build time. Dynamic linking leaves some for the loader. On Linux the format is ELF, on macOS it is Mach-O, and the ideas are identical. Tools: `nm`, `objdump -d`, `readelf` (Linux), `otool` (macOS). **x86-64 and ARM64 differ in encoding and philosophy, not in ideas.** x86 is variable-length, memory operands almost anywhere, decades of accretion. ARM64 is fixed 32-bit instructions, load/store only, 31 general registers. Learning both makes the concept of "ISA" abstract in your head, which is what you want before RISC-V shows up in phase 5. **The ARM64 calling convention on your Mac.** Arguments go in `x0` to `x7` and the return value in `x0`. `bl` puts the return address in the link register `x30` instead of pushing it on the stack. A function that calls another function must save `x30` itself, usually with `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!` at the top and `ldp x29, x30, [sp], #16` before `ret`. `x29` is the frame pointer and `sp` stays 16-byte aligned. Apple differs from Linux in a few spots: `x18` is reserved, variadic arguments (the ones `printf` takes) go on the stack, C symbols get a leading underscore (`_main`), and a syscall is `svc #0x80` with its number in `x16`. ``` int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } x86-64, Linux (-O2) ARM64, macOS (-O2) add: _add: lea eax, [rdi + rsi] add w0, w1, w0 ret ret ``` ### Week by week | Week | Read | Build | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Smith chapters 1 to 7, through HelloSilicon | Assembly 101 on ARM64, natively on the Mac. By hand: a hello world that uses only the `write` and `exit` syscalls, `strlen`, `memcpy`, a loop that sums an array, and a recursive `fib`. Call each one from a C `main` and step through it in `lldb`. | | 2 | Jorgensen, the chapters on instructions, control flow, functions and system services | The same five programs in x86-64, in the Linux VM, with nasm and gdb. Put both versions side by side and write down where the arguments live, how the return address is saved and how the stack is aligned. | | 3 to 4 | Computer Enhance 8086 interlude, first half | 8086 decoder in C. Feed it the course's listings, produce byte-identical reassembly via `nasm`. | | 5 | Computer Enhance second half | 8086 simulator: registers, flags, memory, jumps. Run the course's programs. Print estimated cycles. | | 6 | CS:APP chapter 3, sections 3.1 to 3.8 | Bomb Lab in the Linux VM. Pure disassembly reading, no source. | | 7 | CS:APP 3.10 (buffer overflow), chapter 7 | Attack Lab. Then build your phase 2 JSON parser as three `.o` files linked through `clang`. Inspect the driver's `ld` invocation and identify its runtime inputs. Read the ELF with `readelf -a`. | | 8 | ARM A64 guide chapters on registers, load/store and branches, Apple's ARM64 ABI page | Read clang's ARM64 output at `-O0` and `-O2` for your phase 2 arena and JSON parser. Pick one hot function, rewrite it by hand in ARM64, and benchmark it against clang's version. | ### Project checklist - [ ] The five week 1 programs run on ARM64 (Mac) and x86-64 (VM), written by hand and called from C - [ ] You can write an assembly function that calls another function on both ISAs and explain every stack adjustment in it - [ ] 8086 decoder round-trips every listing in the course - [ ] Simulator runs the course programs with matching register and flag state - [ ] Bomb Lab all six phases defused; Attack Lab at least through level 3 - [ ] You can draw the stack frame of a recursive C function from its disassembly, without running it - [ ] You can explain what `-O2` changed in a 30-line function, instruction by instruction - [ ] You can read clang's ARM64 output at `-O2` as easily as its x86-64 output ### Traps - Do not learn assembly by writing large programs in it. Read a lot, write a little. The compiler writes assembly, you read it. - Do not memorize the x86 instruction set. Learn the 30 instructions that account for 95% of compiled code: `mov, lea, add, sub, imul, and, or, xor, shl, shr, cmp, test, jmp, jcc, call, ret, push, pop, movs/movz, cmov, setcc` plus the SSE moves and arithmetic.

chapters.title: memory hierarchy, performance-aware programming, data-oriented design, SIMD
chapters.goal: explain a hot loop's bottleneck with measurements and a simple cost model. Measure cache effects, branch prediction, arithmetic and memory bandwidth on your hardware. Improve a correct program, then explain the remaining gap. A 100x speedup is a stretch experiment when the baseline contains that much waste, not a requirement to manufacture a slow baseline.
chapters.introHtml:
Goal: explain a hot loop's bottleneck with measurements and a simple cost model. Measure cache effects, branch prediction, arithmetic and memory bandwidth on your hardware. Improve a correct program, then explain the remaining gap. A 100x speedup is a stretch experiment when the baseline contains that much waste, not a requirement to manufacture a slow baseline.

Builds on: phase 3 (reading compiler output). Adds: caches, profiling, SIMD, data-oriented design.

sections.title: Primary resources
sections.html:
• Casey Muratori, Computer Enhance, parts 2 to 4 ("Profiling and measurement", "Moving data", "Reading and writing data with SIMD and cache"). The haversine project runs through the whole course. Do every homework. This is the spine of the phase.
  • Sergey Slotin, Algorithms for Modern Hardware, https://en.algorithmica.org/hpc/. Free, and the best written treatment of caches, SIMD, branchless code and memory-bound algorithms. Chapters on the CPU pipeline, memory, SIMD and "algorithm case studies". Read it alongside the course.
  • MIT 6.172 Performance Engineering of Software Systems (Fall 2018, OCW, https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-172-performance-engineering-of-software-systems-fall-2018/). Lectures 1, 2, 4, 5, 9, 10, 14 and the matrix multiplication homework. Leiserson's lecture 1 takes a 4096³ matmul from 21,000 seconds in Python to 0.4 seconds in C, step by step. Watch it in week 1.
  • Ulrich Drepper, "What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory" (2007, https://www.akkadia.org/drepper/cpumemory.pdf). Sections 2 to 6 only. Use it for the model, not as a specification of today's CPUs. Measure current cache topology, latency and bandwidth yourself.
  • Talks, one each: Mike Acton, "Data-Oriented Design and C++" (CppCon 2014), second viewing, now you will get it. Andrew Kelley, "A Practical Guide to Applying Data-Oriented Design" (Handmade Seattle 2021). Casey Muratori, "Simple Code, High Performance" (2021, the refterm talk).
  • Reference: Agner Fog's optimization manuals, https://www.agner.org/optimize/, manual 1 (optimizing C++) and 3 (microarchitecture). Look things up, do not read cover to cover. Also the uops.info instruction tables for latencies and throughputs.

sections.title: What you are actually learning
sections.html:
The memory hierarchy often sets the limit. Illustrative numbers for an x86-like core, not specifications for your Mac:

                       size        latency      what fits
  registers            ~1 KB       varies      instruction-dependent access/compute cost
  L1 data cache        32-64 KB    ~4 cycles    your hot loop's working set
  L2                   1-2 MB     ~14 cycles    a small table
  L3 (shared)         16-64 MB    ~50 cycles    a medium table
  DRAM                 GBs      ~80-100 ns      everything else (~300 cycles)
  SSD                  TBs      ~50-100 us      ...

  this example assumes 64-byte lines. query your CPU: Apple Silicon differs.

A loop that touches memory in order and uses every byte it fetches runs at DRAM bandwidth, tens of GB/s. A loop that chases pointers pays 100 ns per hop and runs at maybe 10 million hops per second. That is a 100x gap from data layout alone, before any algorithmic cleverness. Dependent loads, poor locality, allocation overhead and branch behavior can all contribute. A pooled tree or a tiny list can behave differently; measure the actual workload.

Array of structs versus struct of arrays. The concrete form of "data-oriented design":

  AoS: struct { float x, y, z, mass; int id; char name[32]; } particles[N];

       memory: [x y z m id name....][x y z m id name....][x y z m id ...
       to update every x you fetch 52 bytes per particle and use 4.

  SoA: struct { float *x, *y, *z, *mass; int *id; char (*name)[32]; } particles;

       memory: [x x x x x x x x x x x x ...][y y y y y ...][z z z ...]
       to update every x you fetch 64 bytes and use 64. 16 floats per line.
       and the compiler can vectorize it.

Acton's talk is 90 minutes on this one idea and its consequences. Kelley's talk shows the practical moves: shrink structs, replace pointers with 32-bit indices into arrays, store the variant tag in a separate array, put the rare fields in a side table.

Branches are predicted, and a mispredict costs about 15 cycles. Sorted data with a if (x > 128) branch is fast, random data is slow, and a branchless version may help unpredictable data. It can also do extra work or lengthen dependencies. Inspect whether the compiler emitted a branch and measure all variants; source syntax alone does not decide. Algorithmica's chapter on branchless programming is the reference.

SIMD does 4, 8 or 16 lanes per instruction.

  scalar:   a[0]+b[0]   a[1]+b[1]   a[2]+b[2]   a[3]+b[3]     4 instructions

  SIMD:     ┌ a0 a1 a2 a3 ┐   ┌ b0 b1 b2 b3 ┐   ┌ a0+b0 a1+b1 a2+b2 a3+b3 ┐
            └────────────┘ + └────────────┘ = └────────────────────────┘   1 instruction
                 128-bit register (SSE / NEON), 4 floats
                 256-bit (AVX2) = 8 floats, 512-bit (AVX-512) = 16

The compiler auto-vectorizes simple loops over SoA data. For everything else you write intrinsics: _mm256_add_ps on x86, vaddq_f32 on ARM NEON. Your Mac supports NEON; native x86 support for SSE/AVX depends on the CPU. Emulated instruction availability is not a performance guarantee. Learn the shared lane model, then check each ISA's alignment, mask, shuffle and tail-handling rules.

Measure with a profiler, a repeatable timer and a model. Start with a monotonic OS clock. Report both minimum and median across repeated runs, plus outliers when latency matters. Raw counters are a later exercise: invariant x86 TSC ticks and ARM cntvct_el0 timer ticks are not current-frequency CPU cycles. Learn frequency conversion, ordering and measurement overhead before using them. A profiler identifies where time goes; a bandwidth or throughput model helps explain why.

Non-pessimization before optimization. Casey's ordering: first do not write slow code (no allocation per element, no virtual dispatch per element, no pointer chasing, no copying you do not need). That gets you 10x to 100x on typical code. Then, only for the hot loop, actual optimization: SIMD, cache blocking, prefetching. Most programs never need the second step.

sections.title: Beginner bridge: correctness and units before speed
sections.html:
Use the same inputs and outputs for every version. Record CPU, OS, compiler, flags, data size, warm/cold state and whether file I/O is timed. Consume a result checksum so the compiler cannot delete the benchmark; inspect optimized assembly when in doubt. Time optimized, non-sanitized builds only after testing.

bandwidth estimate = bytes moved / seconds
throughput         = operations / seconds
arithmetic intensity = operations / bytes moved
rough lower bound  = max(bytes / bandwidth, operations / compute throughput)

This lower bound ignores dependencies and overhead, so failing to reach it is a question to investigate, not proof your code is bad. Cache traffic can exceed your source-level byte count.

For haversine, specify coordinate ranges and an absolute/relative error policy against a double-precision reference. Test identical, nearby and nearly antipodal points. Replacing strtod with a parser for your generator's limited format is valid only if you state that narrower contract. NEON/AVX arithmetic does not directly provide vector sin and asin; use an identified vector-math implementation or a tested approximation, and account for its error.

For SIMD, first add two arrays. Then handle a length that is not a multiple of the lane count without reading past the end. Keep the scalar implementation as the oracle. Run x86 timing on the native laptop, ARM timing on the Mac. An x86 emulator measures its translated execution, not an Intel/AMD microarchitecture.

sections.title: Week by week
sections.html:
Week Read or watch Build
1 6.172 lecture 1, Computer Enhance part 2 start Haversine generator and naive parser (reuse your phase 2 JSON parser). Measure. It is slow.
2 Computer Enhance part 2 Your own block profiler with a monotonic clock, then a repetition tester. Raw-counter timing is a follow-up. Instrument the haversine pipeline.
3 Drepper sections 2 to 4, Algorithmica "Memory" chapter Cache latency and bandwidth probes: measure the cache levels and DRAM available on your native Mac and native x86 laptop. Plot them. Your numbers, not the table above.
4 Computer Enhance part 3, Acton talk again Rewrite the haversine parser to touch each byte once, arena-allocated, no strtod. Target 10x.
5 Algorithmica "Branchless" and "Pipelining" chapters Branch prediction probes. Sorted vs unsorted array sum. Branchless variant. Confirm with perf stat.
6 Kelley talk, Algorithmica hash table chapter Redo your phase 2 hash map: SoA, 32-bit indices, no per-entry allocation, linear probing. Benchmark old vs new at 1M keys.
7 Computer Enhance part 4, Algorithmica SIMD chapter Hand-vectorize the haversine math with NEON intrinsics on the Mac and AVX2 on a supporting native x86 CPU. Compare to clang's auto-vectorization.
8 6.172 lectures 4, 5, 14 Matrix multiply: naive, loop reorder, blocking for L1 and L2, SIMD. Aim for 50% of peak FLOPS. This is the warmup for phase 8.
9 Agner Fog manual 3, chapters on the out-of-order core Microbenchmark instruction latency vs throughput (dependent adds vs independent adds). Understand ILP from your own numbers.
10 nothing new The project: a correct, profiled haversine pipeline with a reproducible before/after comparison. Under 100 ms for 10M points is a hardware- and format-dependent stretch goal. Write the 200-word Sunday note as a full retrospective.

sections.title: Project checklist
sections.html:
• Haversine pipeline has a verified output, repeated before/after timings and a written bottleneck explanation; 100x is stretch
  • A profiler and repetition tester you wrote and will reuse in phases 5, 7 and 8
  • Cache and branch probes with plots of your hardware's real numbers
  • SoA hash table compared at a stated load factor, hit/miss mix and key distribution; explain the result, including regressions
  • Correct blocked SIMD matmul with a throughput model; 50% of a clearly defined one-core peak is stretch

sections.title: Traps
sections.html:
• Do not trust -O3 or the compiler to save you. Look at the assembly. Half of "vectorized" loops are not.
  • Do not infer native hardware performance from cross-ISA emulation. A same-ISA VM is useful for API work, but counters and scheduling can still differ from the host. State which environment each measurement used.
  • Do not optimize before measuring. The profiler comes in week 2 for a reason.

chapters.project: A measured haversine pipeline, SoA hash table and blocked SIMD matmul.
chapters.core: Correct outputs, repeatable measurements and one explained improvement. Speedup ratios are experiments, not grades.

units.title: Baseline, timing, and profiling
units.outcome: Measure a correct baseline reproducibly, report inputs/compiler/hardware, and identify the hot stage before changing code.

read.title: Algorithmica: Instrumentation
read.scope: Timing code regions, instrumentation costs and performance counters. Use a monotonic OS clock before attempting raw counters.
read.why: A written measurement method you can implement and test on your Mac.

visual.title: Computer Enhance: profiler demonstrations
visual.scope: Select the initial profiler/repetition-tester material for your haversine stage. The link is the subscriber index, not a guessed episode URL.
visual.why: Watch the tool being built only if the measurement text leaves an implementation gap.
visual.access: Existing subscription; lesson access not tested

units.build: Build the haversine generator/parser baseline, repetition tester and simple block profiler. Record CPU, OS, compiler, flags, data size, checksum, median and minimum.
units.stop: Stop before optimization until output is checked and the measured hot stage is named. Do not time sanitizer builds or include file I/O accidentally.

units.title: Cache hierarchy and memory access
units.outcome: Measure cache/DRAM behavior on native hardware and explain locality and bandwidth with measured data.

read.title: Algorithms for Modern Hardware: Memory Hierarchy
read.scope: Read the Memory Hierarchy chapter; use it only for the cache and memory hierarchy concepts measured in phase probes.
read.why: It is a concise written model to compare against measured Apple Silicon and native x86 results.
read.access: Free online text; chapter navigation is on the linked index

units.build: Write sequential bandwidth and dependent pointer-chase probes; measure cache working sets on the Mac and, only on native x86 hardware, the x86 laptop.
units.stop: Stop with plotted measurements and a stated machine/compiler setup. Do not treat illustrative latency tables as hardware specifications or use emulation for performance claims.

units.title: Branch behavior
units.outcome: Explain predictable and unpredictable branch costs using measured results.

read.title: Algorithms for Modern Hardware: The Cost of Branching
read.scope: The Cost of Branching only. Compare predictable and unpredictable input; inspect whether clang actually emitted a branch.
read.why: The text gives a model for why branch predictability changes performance without adding another full course.
read.access: Free online text; chapter navigation is on the linked index

units.build: Compare sorted and randomized input with branchful and branchless variants. Inspect optimized code, benchmark identical inputs and explain wins or regressions.
units.stop: Stop when the measurement has a plausible bottleneck explanation. Do not adopt branchless code or SoA on style alone.

units.title: Data layout on the same workload
units.outcome: Choose AoS or SoA based on which fields the operation touches.

read.title: Algorithmica: AoS and SoA
read.scope: This one case study. Compare its pointer-chasing workload with your linear scans rather than assuming SoA always wins.
read.why: The contrasting result forces you to reason about access patterns, not style.

units.build: Convert your phase 2 hash table to contiguous metadata/indices. Compare hit and miss probes at a fixed load factor and key distribution. Also compare a scan using all fields with one using a single field.
units.stop: State bytes touched, measured timings and why each layout won or lost on this workload.

units.title: SIMD and the final measured project
units.outcome: Vectorize array addition and the chosen hot loop while preserving a scalar oracle and testing tail lengths.

read.title: Algorithmica: Intrinsics and Vector Types
read.scope: Vector lanes, loads/stores and intrinsic examples. Its code is x86-oriented: translate the lane model to ARM NEON rather than copying AVX on your Mac.
read.why: A bounded written SIMD model; use native-ISA documentation for the exact operations.

visual.title: Computer Enhance: data movement and SIMD
visual.scope: Only the demonstration matching your current cache/SIMD probe. Skip already-understood measurement lessons.

chapters.sourceText:
Goal: explain a hot loop's bottleneck with measurements and a simple cost model. Measure cache effects, branch prediction, arithmetic and memory bandwidth on your hardware. Improve a correct program, then explain the remaining gap. A 100x speedup is a stretch experiment when the baseline contains that much waste, not a requirement to manufacture a slow baseline.

**Builds on:** phase 3 (reading compiler output). **Adds:** caches, profiling, SIMD, data-oriented design.

### Primary resources

- **Casey Muratori, Computer Enhance, parts 2 to 4** ("Profiling and measurement", "Moving data", "Reading and writing data with SIMD and cache"). The haversine project runs through the whole course. Do every homework. This is the spine of the phase.
- **Sergey Slotin, *Algorithms for Modern Hardware***, https://en.algorithmica.org/hpc/. Free, and the best written treatment of caches, SIMD, branchless code and memory-bound algorithms. Chapters on the CPU pipeline, memory, SIMD and "algorithm case studies". Read it alongside the course.
- **MIT 6.172 Performance Engineering of Software Systems** (Fall 2018, OCW, https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-172-performance-engineering-of-software-systems-fall-2018/). Lectures 1, 2, 4, 5, 9, 10, 14 and the matrix multiplication homework. Leiserson's lecture 1 takes a 4096³ matmul from 21,000 seconds in Python to 0.4 seconds in C, step by step. Watch it in week 1.
- **Ulrich Drepper, "What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory"** (2007, https://www.akkadia.org/drepper/cpumemory.pdf). Sections 2 to 6 only. Use it for the model, not as a specification of today's CPUs. Measure current cache topology, latency and bandwidth yourself.
- **Talks, one each:** Mike Acton, "Data-Oriented Design and C++" (CppCon 2014), second viewing, now you will get it. Andrew Kelley, "A Practical Guide to Applying Data-Oriented Design" (Handmade Seattle 2021). Casey Muratori, "Simple Code, High Performance" (2021, the refterm talk).
- **Reference:** Agner Fog's optimization manuals, https://www.agner.org/optimize/, manual 1 (optimizing C++) and 3 (microarchitecture). Look things up, do not read cover to cover. Also the uops.info instruction tables for latencies and throughputs.

### What you are actually learning

**The memory hierarchy often sets the limit.** Illustrative numbers for an x86-like core, not specifications for your Mac:

```
                       size        latency      what fits
  registers            ~1 KB       varies      instruction-dependent access/compute cost
  L1 data cache        32-64 KB    ~4 cycles    your hot loop's working set
  L2                   1-2 MB     ~14 cycles    a small table
  L3 (shared)         16-64 MB    ~50 cycles    a medium table
  DRAM                 GBs      ~80-100 ns      everything else (~300 cycles)
  SSD                  TBs      ~50-100 us      ...

  this example assumes 64-byte lines. query your CPU: Apple Silicon differs.
```

A loop that touches memory in order and uses every byte it fetches runs at DRAM bandwidth, tens of GB/s. A loop that chases pointers pays 100 ns per hop and runs at maybe 10 million hops per second. That is a 100x gap from data layout alone, before any algorithmic cleverness. Dependent loads, poor locality, allocation overhead and branch behavior can all contribute. A pooled tree or a tiny list can behave differently; measure the actual workload.

**Array of structs versus struct of arrays.** The concrete form of "data-oriented design":

```
  AoS: struct { float x, y, z, mass; int id; char name[32]; } particles[N];

       memory: [x y z m id name....][x y z m id name....][x y z m id ...
       to update every x you fetch 52 bytes per particle and use 4.

  SoA: struct { float *x, *y, *z, *mass; int *id; char (*name)[32]; } particles;

       memory: [x x x x x x x x x x x x ...][y y y y y ...][z z z ...]
       to update every x you fetch 64 bytes and use 64. 16 floats per line.
       and the compiler can vectorize it.
```

Acton's talk is 90 minutes on this one idea and its consequences. Kelley's talk shows the practical moves: shrink structs, replace pointers with 32-bit indices into arrays, store the variant tag in a separate array, put the rare fields in a side table.

**Branches are predicted, and a mispredict costs about 15 cycles.** Sorted data with a `if (x > 128)` branch is fast, random data is slow, and a branchless version may help unpredictable data. It can also do extra work or lengthen dependencies. Inspect whether the compiler emitted a branch and measure all variants; source syntax alone does not decide. Algorithmica's chapter on branchless programming is the reference.

**SIMD does 4, 8 or 16 lanes per instruction.**

```
  scalar:   a[0]+b[0]   a[1]+b[1]   a[2]+b[2]   a[3]+b[3]     4 instructions

  SIMD:     ┌ a0 a1 a2 a3 ┐   ┌ b0 b1 b2 b3 ┐   ┌ a0+b0 a1+b1 a2+b2 a3+b3 ┐
            └────────────┘ + └────────────┘ = └────────────────────────┘   1 instruction
                 128-bit register (SSE / NEON), 4 floats
                 256-bit (AVX2) = 8 floats, 512-bit (AVX-512) = 16
```

The compiler auto-vectorizes simple loops over SoA data. For everything else you write intrinsics: `_mm256_add_ps` on x86, `vaddq_f32` on ARM NEON. Your Mac supports NEON; native x86 support for SSE/AVX depends on the CPU. Emulated instruction availability is not a performance guarantee. Learn the shared lane model, then check each ISA's alignment, mask, shuffle and tail-handling rules.

**Measure with a profiler, a repeatable timer and a model.** Start with a monotonic OS clock. Report both minimum and median across repeated runs, plus outliers when latency matters. Raw counters are a later exercise: invariant x86 TSC ticks and ARM `cntvct_el0` timer ticks are not current-frequency CPU cycles. Learn frequency conversion, ordering and measurement overhead before using them. A profiler identifies where time goes; a bandwidth or throughput model helps explain why.

**Non-pessimization before optimization.** Casey's ordering: first do not write slow code (no allocation per element, no virtual dispatch per element, no pointer chasing, no copying you do not need). That gets you 10x to 100x on typical code. Then, only for the hot loop, actual optimization: SIMD, cache blocking, prefetching. Most programs never need the second step.

### Beginner bridge: correctness and units before speed

Use the same inputs and outputs for every version. Record CPU, OS, compiler, flags, data size, warm/cold state and whether file I/O is timed. Consume a result checksum so the compiler cannot delete the benchmark; inspect optimized assembly when in doubt. Time optimized, non-sanitized builds only after testing.

```text
bandwidth estimate = bytes moved / seconds
throughput         = operations / seconds
arithmetic intensity = operations / bytes moved
rough lower bound  = max(bytes / bandwidth, operations / compute throughput)
```

This lower bound ignores dependencies and overhead, so failing to reach it is a question to investigate, not proof your code is bad. Cache traffic can exceed your source-level byte count.

For haversine, specify coordinate ranges and an absolute/relative error policy against a double-precision reference. Test identical, nearby and nearly antipodal points. Replacing `strtod` with a parser for your generator's limited format is valid only if you state that narrower contract. NEON/AVX arithmetic does not directly provide vector `sin` and `asin`; use an identified vector-math implementation or a tested approximation, and account for its error.

For SIMD, first add two arrays. Then handle a length that is not a multiple of the lane count without reading past the end. Keep the scalar implementation as the oracle. Run x86 timing on the native laptop, ARM timing on the Mac. An x86 emulator measures its translated execution, not an Intel/AMD microarchitecture.

### Week by week

| Week | Read or watch | Build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 6.172 lecture 1, Computer Enhance part 2 start | Haversine generator and naive parser (reuse your phase 2 JSON parser). Measure. It is slow. |
| 2 | Computer Enhance part 2 | Your own block profiler with a monotonic clock, then a repetition tester. Raw-counter timing is a follow-up. Instrument the haversine pipeline. |
| 3 | Drepper sections 2 to 4, Algorithmica "Memory" chapter | Cache latency and bandwidth probes: measure the cache levels and DRAM available on your native Mac and native x86 laptop. Plot them. Your numbers, not the table above. |
| 4 | Computer Enhance part 3, Acton talk again | Rewrite the haversine parser to touch each byte once, arena-allocated, no `strtod`. Target 10x. |
| 5 | Algorithmica "Branchless" and "Pipelining" chapters | Branch prediction probes. Sorted vs unsorted array sum. Branchless variant. Confirm with `perf stat`. |
| 6 | Kelley talk, Algorithmica hash table chapter | Redo your phase 2 hash map: SoA, 32-bit indices, no per-entry allocation, linear probing. Benchmark old vs new at 1M keys. |
| 7 | Computer Enhance part 4, Algorithmica SIMD chapter | Hand-vectorize the haversine math with NEON intrinsics on the Mac and AVX2 on a supporting native x86 CPU. Compare to clang's auto-vectorization. |
| 8 | 6.172 lectures 4, 5, 14 | Matrix multiply: naive, loop reorder, blocking for L1 and L2, SIMD. Aim for 50% of peak FLOPS. This is the warmup for phase 8. |
| 9 | Agner Fog manual 3, chapters on the out-of-order core | Microbenchmark instruction latency vs throughput (dependent adds vs independent adds). Understand ILP from your own numbers. |
| 10 | nothing new | **The project:** a correct, profiled haversine pipeline with a reproducible before/after comparison. Under 100 ms for 10M points is a hardware- and format-dependent stretch goal. Write the 200-word Sunday note as a full retrospective. |

### Project checklist

- [ ] Haversine pipeline has a verified output, repeated before/after timings and a written bottleneck explanation; 100x is stretch
- [ ] A profiler and repetition tester you wrote and will reuse in phases 5, 7 and 8
- [ ] Cache and branch probes with plots of your hardware's real numbers
- [ ] SoA hash table compared at a stated load factor, hit/miss mix and key distribution; explain the result, including regressions
- [ ] Correct blocked SIMD matmul with a throughput model; 50% of a clearly defined one-core peak is stretch

### Traps

- **Do not trust `-O3` or the compiler to save you.** Look at the assembly. Half of "vectorized" loops are not.
- **Do not infer native hardware performance from cross-ISA emulation.** A same-ISA VM is useful for API work, but counters and scheduling can still differ from the host. State which environment each measurement used.
- **Do not optimize before measuring.** The profiler comes in week 2 for a reason.

chapters.title: operating systems, xv6, syscalls, virtual memory, filesystems, sockets

Processes, threads, virtual memory, the page table walk, the scheduler, the filesystem, the syscall boundary. Then use that knowledge from userspace: your own shell, your own malloc, your own event loop on `epoll` and `kqueue`.

sections.title: Primary resources
sections.html:
• OSTEP, Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, Arpaci-Dusseau, free at https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/\~remzi/OSTEP/. The best OS textbook, and short chapters. Virtualization (chapters 3 to 24), concurrency (25 to 34, but phase 6 covers this deeper), persistence (35 to 45).
  • MIT 6.1810 Operating System Engineering, use the archived Fall 2025 offering at https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.1810/2025/, labs on the xv6-riscv kernel, https://github.com/mit-pdos/xv6-riscv. Use that offering's lab repository, book and toolchain together. Lab names and counts change between years; the weekly topic map below is not its exact assignment calendar. Read the xv6 book (PDF on the course site) chapter by chapter with the labs. RISC-V is a third ISA for you and it is the simplest of the three. Runs on QEMU in your Linux VM.
  • Michael Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface (2010). The userspace reference. You do not read it, you look things up: file I/O, processes, signals, mmap, sockets, epoll. It is still the standard because the interface has not changed.
  • Beej's Guide to Network Programming, current online edition at https://beej.us/guide/bgnet/. Free, short, and the only sockets tutorial you need.
  • Talk: Casey Muratori, "The Thirty Million Line Problem" (2015). On what all this OS code costs and why it exists.

sections.title: What you are actually learning
sections.html:
The kernel's job is to multiplex hardware and to lie convincingly. Every process believes it has the whole CPU (the scheduler switches them thousands of times a second) and the whole address space (virtual memory maps it onto scattered physical pages). The lie is enforced by the CPU: user mode cannot touch page tables or devices, so the only way to do anything real is a syscall, which is a controlled trap into the kernel.

xv6 lab "system calls" makes you add one. After that, the boundary is not mysterious.

A process moves between three states, and the scheduler makes every transition:

Virtual memory is a tree lookup done by hardware.

  virtual address (RISC-V Sv39, 39 bits used)
  ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬──────────────┐
  │ L2 (9b) │ L1 (9b) │ L0 (9b) │ offset (12b) │
  └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴──────────────┘

Each entry holds a physical page number and flags (valid, readable, writable, executable, user). The TLB caches recent translations, so most accesses skip the walk.

A TLB miss can require one three-level Sv39 page-table walk, with intermediate entries potentially cached. The TLB usually avoids this walk. A TLB miss costs tens to hundreds of cycles. This is why phase 4 said "touch memory in order": you also stay on the same 4 KB page. And it is why huge pages (2 MB) exist. The "page tables" and "copy-on-write fork" xv6 labs make you build all of this.

A file descriptor is an index into a per-process table of open files. open returns a small integer, the kernel keeps the real state (offset, inode, permissions), and read, write, close, mmap, poll all take that integer. Pipes, sockets, terminals and devices all sit behind the same interface. This uniformity is the Unix idea, and it is why your event loop in week 10 can wait on a socket and a timer with one call.

A filesystem is a data structure on a block device with crash consistency as the hard part. Inodes hold metadata and block pointers, directories map names to inode numbers, a bitmap tracks free blocks, and a log or journal makes multi-block updates atomic across a crash. The xv6 filesystem is 1,000 lines and has all of these. Phase 12 builds a storage engine on top of a filesystem, rather than a filesystem itself.

sections.title: Beginner bridge: ownership crosses the syscall boundary
sections.html:
Before the xv6 labs, read the selected xv6 book's RISC-V register and trap explanation. You already know what an ABI does; now identify a0 to a7, sp, ra, ecall, and the trap-return instruction. Do not translate x86 assembly instruction by instruction.

A descriptor is a resource to close, not memory to free. In a pipeline, draw which process owns every pipe end. Close unused ends after fork; otherwise a reader may never see EOF. Build a foreground command first, then redirection and a two-command pipeline. waitpid, process groups and foreground-terminal control come before full background-job handling.

An event loop starts smaller than HTTP:

accept connection -> nonblocking socket -> wait for readiness
    readable: read some bytes -> append to bounded input buffer
    writable: send queued bytes -> keep any unsent suffix
    EOF/error/timeout: remove from loop -> close -> free state

Readiness means an operation can make progress, not that a complete request has arrived. Handle short reads/writes, EINTR, EAGAIN, EOF and backpressure (stop accepting more work when output cannot drain). Start level-triggered; read epoll(7) before edge-triggering.

Checkpoint: echo works when a client sends one byte at a time, when another stops reading, and when one disconnects mid-message. Other clients still progress. Bound buffers, connection counts and timeouts. Then implement a documented HTTP subset; RFC 9112 sections 2, 3 and 6 specify parsing and message framing. Reject unsupported framing and prevent file paths escaping the serving directory. Keep the learning server on loopback or an isolated lab network.

Nonblocking sockets do not make disk reads nonblocking. Preload a small fixture set first; move disk work off the loop in phase 6. For the allocator, test alignment, splitting, coalescing and realloc semantics in a driver before LD_PRELOAD. Replacing a process allocator also requires compatible calloc/realloc, threading and initialization behavior; Python is a stretch integration test.

sections.title: Week by week
sections.html:
Week Read Build
1 OSTEP 4 to 6, xv6 book chapter 1 and 2 xv6 up in QEMU in your VM. Labs: util (write sleep, pingpong, primes, find, xargs as xv6 user programs).
2 OSTEP 7 to 11, xv6 book chapter 4 Lab: syscall (add tracing and a sysinfo call). Read trap.c and syscall.c line by line.
3 to 4 OSTEP 13 to 20, xv6 book chapter 3 Labs: pgtbl and traps. Draw the xv6 address space and page table on paper.
5 OSTEP 21 to 22 Labs: cow (copy-on-write fork) and lazy or mmap depending on the year's set.
6 OSTEP 26 to 30, xv6 book chapter 6 and 7 Labs: thread and lock. Read proc.c, especially scheduler and swtch.S. Draw a context switch.
7 OSTEP 39 to 42, xv6 book chapter 8 Lab: fs (large files, symlinks). Read fs.c and log.c.
8 TLPI chapters on fork, exec, signals, pipes Userspace project 1: a shell in C on Linux. Pipes, redirection, background jobs, signal handling for Ctrl-C. Use your phase 2 library.
9 OSTEP 17, TLPI on mmap and brk Userspace project 2: a malloc and free on top of mmap. Size classes, free lists, coalescing. Run real programs against it with LD_PRELOAD. Benchmark against glibc with your phase 4 tester.
10 to 11 Beej's guide, TLPI on sockets and epoll Userspace project 3: an event loop with epoll (Linux) and kqueue (macOS) behind one interface. On top of it, a bounded HTTP/1.1 subset server that serves preloaded static files without blocking its event-loop thread. Scale toward 10k connections only after the correctness tests pass. Load test with wrk.
12 OSTEP 36 to 38 (I/O devices, disks) Read the xv6 virtio_disk.c driver. Then read the Linux read syscall path in the kernel source, from ksys_read down to the block layer, with a browser like https://elixir.bootlin.com. Just read.

sections.title: Project checklist
sections.html:
• The selected xv6 labs pass their matching course-year grading scripts; record any deferred labs
  • Shell runs ls | grep c | wc -l > out.txt & correctly
  • Allocator passes its test driver; running python3 or sqlite3 via LD_PRELOAD is stretch
  • HTTP server passes slow-client and disconnect tests; record load-test limits, descriptor limits and latency. 10k connections is stretch
  • You can draw, from memory, the syscall path, the page table walk and a context switch

sections.title: Traps
sections.html:
• Do not read OSTEP end to end first. Each week's chapters unblock that week's lab, in that order.
  • Do not use a thread per connection in the HTTP server. The point is the event loop, and phase 6 will add the threads correctly.
  • Do not port xv6 to your Mac. It runs in QEMU in the Linux VM and that is fine.

chapters.core: Match the xv6 course year's book, lab repo and grading scripts. Slow/disconnected clients must not block other clients. The required traps and mmap integration tests also pass; xv6 scheduling work follows the user-space queue in phase 6.

units.title: Processes, traps, and system calls
units.outcome: Explain the user/kernel boundary and implement one xv6 system call; make a foreground shell run a command with fork, exec, and wait.

read.title: OSTEP: Process API
read.scope: Read the process creation and control API sections, then stop before scheduling.
read.why: A short primary-text account of fork/exec/wait gives the shell a model; the xv6 lab then shows the kernel side.

visual.title: xv6 book: Traps and system calls
visual.scope: Use the trap/system-call diagrams and the matching xv6 RISC-V book section; do not read the full book in advance.
visual.why: The trap path and register handoff are distinct from OSTEP's API narrative and connect directly to the lab code.

units.build: Run the matching Fall 2025 syscall lab and write a foreground shell for one external command. Once it works, draw descriptor ownership and add redirection plus a two-command pipeline; close unused pipe ends after fork. Then complete the matching traps lab and annotate saved registers and the user/supervisor return boundary; a scheduler experiment follows in phase 6 once the pthread queue is working.
units.stop: The selected xv6 tests pass, the shell reaps children, and pipeline EOF/redirection behave correctly. Full background-job control remains stretch.

units.title: Virtual memory and copy-on-write
units.outcome: Trace virtual-to-physical translation and explain why copy-on-write fork delays copying pages.

read.title: OSTEP: Introduction to Paging
read.scope: Chapter 18: page/frame translation and page-table entries. Use the matching xv6 book figures for Sv39 and COW implementation.
read.why: Adds the concrete paging model missing from a general address-space introduction.

visual.title: xv6 book: Page tables
visual.scope: Use the Sv39 page-table walk and address-space figures alongside the pgtbl/cow lab.
visual.why: The concrete RISC-V address fields and xv6 mappings add architecture-specific visual context rather than repeating the OSTEP abstraction.

units.build: Complete the selected pgtbl and cow exercises; diagram one translation and the page reference/copy path for fork.
units.stop: Stop after the course-year tests pass and the COW explanation matches the code. Do not implement a general-purpose allocator here.

units.title: Filesystems and crash consistency
units.outcome: Follow a file operation through inode, block mapping, and log, and explain what the log protects across a crash.

read.title: OSTEP: File System Implementation (chapter 40)
read.scope: Read the inode, directory, and block mapping discussion; use journaling only to understand xv6's log.
read.why: It supplies vocabulary for the xv6 fs lab without requiring all OSTEP persistence chapters.

visual.title: xv6 book: File system
visual.scope: Follow the filesystem layering and logging figures around the matching book section.
visual.why: The xv6-specific layers and transaction path are useful diagrams not covered by the generic OSTEP chapter.

units.build: Complete the selected xv6 fs exercise and annotate one create/write path from syscall to on-disk blocks.
units.stop: Stop at the selected lab's tests. Do not build a filesystem or read Linux block-layer source as a prerequisite.

units.title: Lazy file mappings and their lifetime
units.outcome: Tie page faults, file references, permissions, unmapping and fork together in xv6.

read.title: xv6 Fall 2025: mmap lab
read.scope: The required mmap/munmap subset and hints only. Skip optional shared-physical-page/unified-buffer-cache challenges.
read.why: This is a new VM/filesystem integration build; it does not repeat the userspace mmap allocator.

units.build: Implement lazy file-backed mmap/munmap, permission checks, MAP_SHARED writeback, and exit/fork reference handling. Run mmaptest and usertests -q; add a protection or reference-lifetime regression test.
units.stop: Both test programs pass and you can trace one fault from VMA lookup to file data and PTE; file references survive descriptor close and are released on unmap/exit.

units.title: A tested userspace allocator
units.outcome: Split and coalesce free blocks without violating alignment or allocation ownership.

read.title: OSTEP: Free-Space Management
read.scope: Chapter 17: tracking free space, splitting, coalescing and placement policies. Skip kernel-specific policy detours.
read.why: This is the allocator mechanism needed by the existing project, not another C memory introduction.

units.build: Build malloc/free over an mmap-backed region in a dedicated test driver. Test alignment, splitting, coalescing, allocation failure and realloc semantics before attempting interposition.
units.stop: The isolated driver passes without lost or overlapping blocks. LD_PRELOAD and replacement of a production allocator remain stretch.

units.title: Bounded nonblocking I/O
units.outcome: Write an echo server that handles partial I/O, a slow reader, and disconnects without blocking other clients.

read.title: Beej's Guide to Network Programming
read.scope: Use the client/server, select/poll, and partial-send discussions; skip unrelated protocol examples.
read.why: A focused sockets reference is more useful here than the broad TLPI volume; the project exercises the actual API contract.

units.build: Implement a level-triggered epoll echo loop with bounded per-client buffers, then test one-byte writes, stalled readers, and mid-message closes. After echo passes, implement the roadmap’s bounded HTTP subset for preloaded fixtures; reject unsupported framing.
units.stop: Slow/disconnected clients do not block others and the documented HTTP subset passes framing/bounds tests. kqueue portability and load targets are follow-ons.

chapters.weekHtml:
Week Read Build
1 OSTEP 4 to 6, xv6 book chapter 1 and 2 xv6 up in QEMU in your VM. Labs: util (write sleep, pingpong, primes, find, xargs as xv6 user programs).
2 OSTEP 7 to 11, xv6 book chapter 4 Lab: syscall (add tracing and a sysinfo call). Read trap.c and syscall.c line by line.
3 to 4 OSTEP 13 to 20, xv6 book chapter 3 Labs: pgtbl and traps. Draw the xv6 address space and page table on paper.
5 OSTEP 21 to 22 Labs: cow (copy-on-write fork) and lazy or mmap depending on the year's set.
6 OSTEP 26 to 30, xv6 book chapter 6 and 7 Labs: thread and lock. Read proc.c, especially scheduler and swtch.S. Draw a context switch.
7 OSTEP 39 to 42, xv6 book chapter 8 Lab: fs (large files, symlinks). Read fs.c and log.c.
8 TLPI chapters on fork, exec, signals, pipes Userspace project 1: a shell in C on Linux. Pipes, redirection, background jobs, signal handling for Ctrl-C. Use your phase 2 library.
9 OSTEP 17, TLPI on mmap and brk Userspace project 2: a malloc and free on top of mmap. Size classes, free lists, coalescing. Run real programs against it with LD_PRELOAD. Benchmark against glibc with your phase 4 tester.
10 to 11 Beej's guide, TLPI on sockets and epoll Userspace project 3: an event loop with epoll (Linux) and kqueue (macOS) behind one interface. On top of it, a bounded HTTP/1.1 subset server that serves preloaded static files without blocking its event-loop thread. Scale toward 10k connections only after the correctness tests pass. Load test with wrk.
12 OSTEP 36 to 38 (I/O devices, disks) Read the xv6 virtio_disk.c driver. Then read the Linux read syscall path in the kernel source, from ksys_read down to the block layer, with a browser like https://elixir.bootlin.com. Just read.
chapters.sourceText:
Goal: know what the kernel does for your program, because you modified a real kernel to do it. Processes, threads, virtual memory, the page table walk, the scheduler, the filesystem, the syscall boundary. Then use that knowledge from userspace: your own shell, your own malloc, your own event loop on `epoll` and `kqueue`. **Builds on:** phase 3 (registers, stack frames, calling conventions) and phase 4 (the memory hierarchy). **Adds:** processes, syscalls, virtual memory, filesystems, sockets. ### Primary resources - **OSTEP, *Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces***, Arpaci-Dusseau, free at https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/\~remzi/OSTEP/. The best OS textbook, and short chapters. Virtualization (chapters 3 to 24), concurrency (25 to 34, but phase 6 covers this deeper), persistence (35 to 45). - **MIT 6.1810 Operating System Engineering**, use the archived Fall 2025 offering at https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.1810/2025/, labs on the xv6-riscv kernel, https://github.com/mit-pdos/xv6-riscv. Use that offering's lab repository, book and toolchain together. Lab names and counts change between years; the weekly topic map below is not its exact assignment calendar. Read the xv6 book (PDF on the course site) chapter by chapter with the labs. RISC-V is a third ISA for you and it is the simplest of the three. Runs on QEMU in your Linux VM. - **Michael Kerrisk, *The Linux Programming Interface*** (2010). The userspace reference. You do not read it, you look things up: file I/O, processes, signals, `mmap`, sockets, `epoll`. It is still the standard because the interface has not changed. - **Beej's Guide to Network Programming**, current online edition at https://beej.us/guide/bgnet/. Free, short, and the only sockets tutorial you need. - **Talk:** Casey Muratori, "The Thirty Million Line Problem" (2015). On what all this OS code costs and why it exists. ### What you are actually learning **The kernel's job is to multiplex hardware and to lie convincingly.** Every process believes it has the whole CPU (the scheduler switches them thousands of times a second) and the whole address space (virtual memory maps it onto scattered physical pages). The lie is enforced by the CPU: user mode cannot touch page tables or devices, so the only way to do anything real is a syscall, which is a controlled trap into the kernel. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant U as User process participant L as libc participant K as Kernel U->>L: read(fd, buf, n) L->>K: args in registers, then syscall / ecall / svc Note over K: CPU switches to supervisor mode
and jumps to the trap vector K->>K: save registers to the trapframe K->>K: look up the syscall number, call sys_read K->>K: check the user pointer is valid,
copy file data into user memory K->>L: restore registers, sret / sysret L->>U: byte count, from rax / a0 ``` xv6 lab "system calls" makes you add one. After that, the boundary is not mysterious. A process moves between three states, and the scheduler makes every transition: ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Ready: fork Ready --> Running: scheduled Running --> Ready: timer interrupt Running --> Blocked: waits on I/O Blocked --> Ready: I/O done Running --> [*]: exit ``` **Virtual memory is a tree lookup done by hardware.** ``` virtual address (RISC-V Sv39, 39 bits used) ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬──────────────┐ │ L2 (9b) │ L1 (9b) │ L0 (9b) │ offset (12b) │ └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴──────────────┘ ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR S[satp register] --> R[Root table
512 entries] R -->|L2 picks entry| M[Mid table
512 entries] M -->|L1 picks entry| LF[Leaf table
512 entries] LF -->|L0 picks entry| PP[Physical page
4 KB] PP -->|+ offset| PA[Physical address] ``` Each entry holds a physical page number and flags (valid, readable, writable, executable, user). The TLB caches recent translations, so most accesses skip the walk. A TLB miss can require one three-level Sv39 page-table walk, with intermediate entries potentially cached. The TLB usually avoids this walk. A TLB miss costs tens to hundreds of cycles. This is why phase 4 said "touch memory in order": you also stay on the same 4 KB page. And it is why huge pages (2 MB) exist. The "page tables" and "copy-on-write fork" xv6 labs make you build all of this. **A file descriptor is an index into a per-process table of open files.** `open` returns a small integer, the kernel keeps the real state (offset, inode, permissions), and `read`, `write`, `close`, `mmap`, `poll` all take that integer. Pipes, sockets, terminals and devices all sit behind the same interface. This uniformity is the Unix idea, and it is why your event loop in week 10 can wait on a socket and a timer with one call. **A filesystem is a data structure on a block device with crash consistency as the hard part.** Inodes hold metadata and block pointers, directories map names to inode numbers, a bitmap tracks free blocks, and a log or journal makes multi-block updates atomic across a crash. The xv6 filesystem is 1,000 lines and has all of these. Phase 12 builds a storage engine on top of a filesystem, rather than a filesystem itself. ### Beginner bridge: ownership crosses the syscall boundary Before the xv6 labs, read the selected xv6 book's RISC-V register and trap explanation. You already know what an ABI does; now identify `a0` to `a7`, `sp`, `ra`, `ecall`, and the trap-return instruction. Do not translate x86 assembly instruction by instruction. A descriptor is a resource to close, not memory to free. In a pipeline, draw which process owns every pipe end. Close unused ends after `fork`; otherwise a reader may never see EOF. Build a foreground command first, then redirection and a two-command pipeline. `waitpid`, process groups and foreground-terminal control come before full background-job handling. An event loop starts smaller than HTTP: ```text accept connection -> nonblocking socket -> wait for readiness readable: read some bytes -> append to bounded input buffer writable: send queued bytes -> keep any unsent suffix EOF/error/timeout: remove from loop -> close -> free state ``` Readiness means an operation can make progress, not that a complete request has arrived. Handle short reads/writes, `EINTR`, `EAGAIN`, EOF and backpressure (stop accepting more work when output cannot drain). Start level-triggered; read [epoll(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/epoll.7.html) before edge-triggering. **Checkpoint:** echo works when a client sends one byte at a time, when another stops reading, and when one disconnects mid-message. Other clients still progress. Bound buffers, connection counts and timeouts. Then implement a documented HTTP subset; [RFC 9112 sections 2, 3 and 6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112) specify parsing and message framing. Reject unsupported framing and prevent file paths escaping the serving directory. Keep the learning server on loopback or an isolated lab network. Nonblocking sockets do not make disk reads nonblocking. Preload a small fixture set first; move disk work off the loop in phase 6. For the allocator, test alignment, splitting, coalescing and `realloc` semantics in a driver before `LD_PRELOAD`. Replacing a process allocator also requires compatible `calloc`/`realloc`, threading and initialization behavior; Python is a stretch integration test. ### Week by week | Week | Read | Build | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | OSTEP 4 to 6, xv6 book chapter 1 and 2 | xv6 up in QEMU in your VM. Labs: `util` (write `sleep`, `pingpong`, `primes`, `find`, `xargs` as xv6 user programs). | | 2 | OSTEP 7 to 11, xv6 book chapter 4 | Lab: `syscall` (add tracing and a `sysinfo` call). Read `trap.c` and `syscall.c` line by line. | | 3 to 4 | OSTEP 13 to 20, xv6 book chapter 3 | Labs: `pgtbl` and `traps`. Draw the xv6 address space and page table on paper. | | 5 | OSTEP 21 to 22 | Labs: `cow` (copy-on-write fork) and `lazy` or `mmap` depending on the year's set. | | 6 | OSTEP 26 to 30, xv6 book chapter 6 and 7 | Labs: `thread` and `lock`. Read `proc.c`, especially `scheduler` and `swtch.S`. Draw a context switch. | | 7 | OSTEP 39 to 42, xv6 book chapter 8 | Lab: `fs` (large files, symlinks). Read `fs.c` and `log.c`. | | 8 | TLPI chapters on `fork`, `exec`, signals, pipes | **Userspace project 1:** a shell in C on Linux. Pipes, redirection, background jobs, signal handling for Ctrl-C. Use your phase 2 library. | | 9 | OSTEP 17, TLPI on `mmap` and `brk` | **Userspace project 2:** a `malloc` and `free` on top of `mmap`. Size classes, free lists, coalescing. Run real programs against it with `LD_PRELOAD`. Benchmark against glibc with your phase 4 tester. | | 10 to 11 | Beej's guide, TLPI on sockets and `epoll` | **Userspace project 3:** an event loop with `epoll` (Linux) and `kqueue` (macOS) behind one interface. On top of it, a bounded HTTP/1.1 subset server that serves preloaded static files without blocking its event-loop thread. Scale toward 10k connections only after the correctness tests pass. Load test with `wrk`. | | 12 | OSTEP 36 to 38 (I/O devices, disks) | Read the xv6 `virtio_disk.c` driver. Then read the Linux `read` syscall path in the kernel source, from `ksys_read` down to the block layer, with a browser like https://elixir.bootlin.com. Just read. | ### Project checklist - [ ] The selected xv6 labs pass their matching course-year grading scripts; record any deferred labs - [ ] Shell runs `ls | grep c | wc -l > out.txt &` correctly - [ ] Allocator passes its test driver; running `python3` or `sqlite3` via `LD_PRELOAD` is stretch - [ ] HTTP server passes slow-client and disconnect tests; record load-test limits, descriptor limits and latency. 10k connections is stretch - [ ] You can draw, from memory, the syscall path, the page table walk and a context switch ### Traps - Do not read OSTEP end to end first. Each week's chapters unblock that week's lab, in that order. - Do not use a thread per connection in the HTTP server. The point is the event loop, and phase 6 will add the threads correctly. - Do not port xv6 to your Mac. It runs in QEMU in the Linux VM and that is fine.

chapters.title: concurrency and parallelism, memory models, job systems
chapters.goal: write multithreaded C that is correct under the C11 memory model and fast on a 10-core machine, and know the difference. Ship a work-stealing job system and use it to parallelize your phase 4 haversine and matmul.
chapters.introHtml:
Goal: write multithreaded C that is correct under the C11 memory model and fast on a 10-core machine, and know the difference. Ship a work-stealing job system and use it to parallelize your phase 4 haversine and matmul.

Builds on: phase 4 (cache lines) and phase 5 (threads and the scheduler). Adds: atomics, memory models, locks, job systems.

sections.title: Primary resources
sections.html:
• Mara Bos, Rust Atomics and Locks (2023, free at https://marabos.nl/atomics/). Yes, it is a Rust book, and it is the clearest explanation of atomics, memory ordering, spinlocks, mutexes and condition variables in print. Chapters 1 to 6 and 8 to 9. The concepts are identical in C11 stdatomic.h. Read it now, before you know Rust, and it will make phase 7 easier.
  • Paul McKenney, Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It? (free, use the revision listed at https://cdn.kernel.org/pub/linux/kernel/people/paulmck/perfbook/perfbook.html). Chapters 3 (hardware), 4 (tools), 5 (counting), 7 (locking) and appendix C (memory barriers). McKenney wrote RCU for the Linux kernel. When he says something about cache coherence, it is true.
  • Stanford CS149 Parallel Computing (Fall 2023 lecture videos on YouTube, linked from https://gfxcourses.stanford.edu/cs149/fall25). Lectures 1 to 6 and 10 to 12. Best treatment of the "why is parallel code slow" side: false sharing, load imbalance, Amdahl, work distribution.
  • OSTEP chapters 26 to 34 as the gentle version if Bos and McKenney are too dense.
  • Modern C level 3 for the C11 threads and atomics API itself.

sections.title: What you are actually learning
sections.html:
Cache coherence makes sharing expensive. Cache topology depends on the CPU; for example, some cores share an L2 within a cluster. When two cores write to the same cache line, the line ping-pongs between them at ~100 cycles a bounce. This happens even when they write to different variables that happen to share a line: false sharing.

  core 0 writes counter[0]          core 1 writes counter[1]
         │                                   │
         ▼                                   ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ counter[0] │ counter[1] │ counter[2] │ ... one 64-byte line  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
              the line bounces between the two cores' caches on every write.
              fix: pad each counter to its own line, or give each thread its own
              counter and sum at the end.

The rule that follows: threads should share almost nothing while working, and combine results at the end. That is also why data-oriented layouts parallelize well: split the array into chunks, one per thread, done.

The memory model is about what other threads can observe, not about what your thread does. Compilers and CPUs reorder loads and stores. Within one thread you never notice. Across threads, thread B can see thread A's second write before its first. Atomics with ordering constraints are how you say "no, this write must be visible after that one":

  • release/acquire: when the acquire load observes the release store (or the applicable release sequence), preceding writes become ordered before the acquiring thread's subsequent reads.
  • relaxed: atomic access, without that publication guarantee. Useful for independent counters, not automatically for publishing data.
  • seq_cst: adds a single total order for sequentially consistent atomic operations. A sensible starting point, but it cannot repair an incorrect algorithm.

In the diagram, ready is atomic and data is written once before publication. The acquire must actually read the published true. Without synchronization, the non-atomic accesses to data can form a data race, which is undefined behavior, not merely a stale value. Bos chapter 3 is this diagram, expanded over 40 pages, and worth every one.

A mutex is a flag plus a way to sleep. A spinlock is while (atomic_exchange(&locked, 1)) {}. A real mutex spins briefly then asks the kernel to put the thread to sleep (futex on Linux) so it does not burn a core. You build both in week 2 and measure the difference under contention.

Parallelism is about work distribution. Eight threads do not give 8x. Amdahl says the serial part caps you. Load imbalance means some threads finish early. Synchronization costs cycles. A job system solves the distribution problem generically:

Opposite ends reduce contention on common paths, but empty/last-item transitions still need careful synchronization. Chase-Lev is one work-stealing design, with subtle weak-memory and reclamation requirements. A locked deque is a valid first implementation. Central queues and static partitioning are also useful; choose from measured workload needs.

sections.title: Beginner bridge: make the queue correct before removing locks
sections.html:
Concurrency means operations overlap in time. Parallelism means work actually executes at the same time. A single-core program can have concurrency bugs. A data race is a particular unsynchronized conflicting memory access; a broader race condition can exist even when every access is atomic.

Build in this order: mutex plus condition-variable queue, worker pool, static chunking, bounded single-producer/single-consumer (SPSC) ring, then work stealing with one lock per deque. Wait on a condition-variable predicate in a loop because wakeups do not prove work is available. Only replace the locked deque after you can state its owner/thief rules, linearization points and storage lifetime. Multiple-producer/multiple-consumer (MPMC) lock-free queues are stretch work.

Test every job ID completes exactly once, tiny capacities and wraparound, full/empty transitions, waiting parents, idle shutdown and shutdown with pending work. Give tests timeouts so a deadlock is a failure, not an overnight hang. Compare a locked reference with the more complex version on the same workload.

Use ThreadSanitizer in a separate build from ASan. It detects many executed data races, not lost jobs, every ordering error, deadlock or proof of lock-freedom. Bos supplies the memory-model explanation; do not add a second concurrency course. Read just enough Rust syntax from its introduction to understand examples, and implement them in C with explicit atomics.

sections.title: Week by week
sections.html:
Week Read Build
1 Bos chapters 1 to 3, McKenney chapter 3 Parallel sum with pthread. Atomic shared counter, then adjacent per-thread atomic counters versus padded/aligned per-thread atomic counters using the same loop and memory ordering, then per-thread locals. The adjacent/padded pair isolates false sharing. A deliberately racy counter is a bug demonstration, not a valid speed baseline. Plot speedup vs threads. See false sharing in numbers.
2 Bos chapter 4, McKenney chapter 7 Spinlock, then a futex-based mutex (Linux), then a ticket lock. Benchmark all three at 1, 4, 16 threads with your phase 4 tester.
3 Bos chapters 5 to 6, McKenney chapter 5 Bounded SPSC ring buffer, then a mutex-protected MPMC queue; lock-free MPMC is stretch. Test with ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread). Understand every report it gives you.
4 CS149 lectures 1 to 6 Parallel haversine and parallel blocked matmul using plain threads and static chunking. Measure scaling on all your cores.
5 Bos chapter 8 and 9, the Chase-Lev paper ("Dynamic Circular Work-Stealing Deque", 2005) The project: a work-stealing job system in C. Start with locked deques, a configurable worker count, and a job_wait that helps run jobs. A validated weak-memory Chase-Lev implementation is stretch, not an exercise in guessing fences.
6 CS149 lectures 10 to 12 Move the matmul and the phase 5 HTTP server's request handling onto the job system. Compare with week 4's static split.

sections.title: Project checklist
sections.html:
• Speedup plots for every experiment; explain the adjacent/padded counter result even if this hardware shows no dramatic cliff
  • Ring buffer and queue pass exactly-once, wraparound, shutdown and timeout tests, plus ThreadSanitizer stress with zero reports; record that this is testing, not a correctness proof
  • Job system runs the matmul within 10% of the hand-split version and handles uneven jobs better
  • You can explain acquire/release with the diagram above, from memory, and name where your job system needs each

sections.title: Traps
sections.html:
• Start with locks or seq_cst where appropriate. Weaken an ordering only after writing the required happens-before argument and measuring a reason to change it. Stronger ordering is not a substitute for correct ownership.
  • Do not write lock-free code beyond the ring buffer and the deque. Lock-free is a specialty. Locks with short critical sections are the right default for the rest of your career.
  • ThreadSanitizer is not optional. A data race that never shows up in tests is still UB.

chapters.project: A tested lock-based work-stealing job system and bounded SPSC queue.
chapters.core: Exactly-once completion, wraparound, shutdown and timeout tests. Lock-free MPMC and weak-memory deques are stretch. Complete the small measured xv6 scheduling experiment after the user-space queue works.

units.title: Threads, races, and publication
units.outcome: Create and join pthreads and distinguish thread-local work from unsynchronized shared state.

read.title: OSTEP: Thread API
read.scope: Chapter 27: create/join and pthread API examples. Skip the already-known process API.
read.why: One short C-based introduction avoids learning Rust syntax before using threads.

units.build: Write a parallel sum with private partial results and join before combining them. Run a separate ThreadSanitizer build; do not benchmark deliberately racy code.
units.stop: Each worker owns its partial result until join, the sum matches a scalar oracle and shutdown cannot leave live threads.

units.title: Mutexes, condition variables, and waiting
units.outcome: Build a bounded mutex/condition-variable queue and state its empty/full and shutdown invariants.

read.title: OSTEP: Condition Variables
read.scope: Chapter 30: predicate loops and producer/consumer example. Do not implement a futex or custom mutex yet.
read.why: A direct pthread-based sleep/wake pattern for the bounded queue.

units.build: Implement a small-capacity pthread queue; test empty waits, full queues, wraparound, and shutdown while workers are idle or have pending work.
units.stop: Stop when timeout-bounded tests complete and each submitted item is handled exactly once. A lock-free MPMC queue is not needed.

units.title: Parallel work and load balance
units.outcome: Measure static chunking, false sharing, and imbalance, and explain why thread count does not translate directly to speedup.

read.title: Rust Atomics and Locks: Understanding the Processor (chapter 7)
read.scope: Read the hardware/cache-coherence sections that explain why writes to shared cache lines contend.
read.why: This is a bounded hardware explanation for the false-sharing measurement, separate from the earlier ordering and lock chapters.

visual.title: Stanford CS149: work distribution (index)
visual.scope: From the pinned schedule, choose only the lecture about work distribution/load balance that matches your static-chunking experiment. Do not watch lectures 1–6 as another queue.
visual.why: The lecture demonstrations add visual execution and workload examples alongside the written cache-coherence explanation.

units.build: Compare adjacent and padded per-thread counters, then parallelize a phase 4 workload with static chunks. Record machine, inputs, and timings. After the user-space scaling tests, instrument the pinned xv6 scheduler for runnable/wait time and try one small policy change. Use kernel locks and timer interrupts already studied in phase 5; compare the behavior on a fixed workload, not a host-thread speed claim.
units.stop: Stop when you can account for the observed scaling and false-sharing result, even if the hardware shows no large speed gap.

units.title: Publication and the bounded SPSC ring
units.outcome: Explain how an acquire observation makes a producer’s preceding writes visible.

read.title: Rust Atomics and Locks: Memory Ordering
read.scope: Chapter 3: relaxed versus release/acquire and happens-before. Read enough of the introduction to understand examples; implement in C11.
read.why: Adds the ordering argument needed to replace the simple single-producer/single-consumer path, not another Rust course.

units.build: First test one-time publication. Then build a bounded SPSC ring with one producer and one consumer; test tiny capacity, wraparound, full/empty transitions and timeout-bounded shutdown.
units.stop: Write the release/acquire and storage-lifetime argument, then pass exactly-once and wraparound stress tests. A clean TSan run is not a proof.

units.title: Locked work stealing
units.outcome: Build a job system with worker-local deques, stealing, wait-helping, and explicit shutdown without guessing weak-memory fences.

read.title: Rust Atomics and Locks: Building Our Own Channels (chapter 5), selected
read.scope: Read the channel ownership and synchronization examples only where they clarify job publication and completion.
read.why: The existing book provides targeted patterns; the phase project intentionally keeps deque synchronization with locks.

units.build: Start with a locked deque per worker and a configurable pool; run exactly-once, uneven-job, waiting-parent, and idle-shutdown tests.
units.stop: Stop when correctness and measured comparison against static chunking are complete. Chase-Lev and lock-free MPMC are stretch work.

chapters.rationale: Teach the needed concurrency concepts directly, in C, without making Rust fluency a prerequisite. Bos's freely readable chapters explain atomics and synchronization exceptionally well; use only the sections that support the staged queue/job-system project. CS149 videos add distinct visual explanations of parallel workload behavior, not a second implementation track.

excluded.title: Full Rust course before concurrency
excluded.reason: The phase uses Rust Atomics and Locks as a concept text and implements in C. Rust syntax is not a prerequisite for pthreads or the C11 memory model.

excluded.title: Full McKenney book and full CS149 course
excluded.reason: Both are substantial references. Select only CS149 lectures for the distinct parallel-performance perspective; consult McKenney only if a concrete coherence question remains.
